events.speaker: product_manager
events.message: The UX concern about the browser surfaces is real polish debt, but it doesn't touch the question I'm here to answer, because the browser page is a fallback, not the product. The core flow is app-to-app over the LAN, and the README states the whole promise in one sentence a normal person can repeat. What convinces me anyone would use this is that strangers, not the builder, maintain the distribution: Flathub, AUR, Nixpkgs, Snap, Chocolatey, Scoop and Homebrew each have a named outside maintainer. Nobody spends their weekend packaging a DEB and an RPM for a tool they don't personally run. I'd also push back on the framing that this is a thin AirDrop clone with no stated difference: the differentiator is explicit and it's the reason the project exists at all, namely no Apple hardware lock-in and no external server. One thing I still can't verify from the brief is whether the WebRTC path through that signaling server actually completes a transfer, and that matters because it's the only answer to 'both devices aren't on the same Wi-Fi'.

events.headline: Three reviewers landed on useful (senior engineer, product manager, general user); the UX designer stayed unsure, and no one voted not useful.
agreed: Product manager and general user both treated the plain one-sentence problem statement plus real distribution as settled evidence of demand — third-party packagers across Flathub, AUR, Nixpkgs, Snap, Chocolatey, Scoop and Homebrew, and dozens of community translations.

Senior engineer and product manager agreed the engineering is production-grade: real CI, integration tests that exercise genuine failure modes, pinned toolchains, version-parity checks, and signing keys handled as secrets.

UX designer and general user independently named the same gap: no walkthrough, video, or screenshot sequence exists showing a first-time user picking files and completing a send, so the moment value lands is asserted rather than shown.
split: Whether the browser surfaces count: UX designer argued the CLI help text advertises share-via-link as a first-class hotkey, making the download page a documented path with real dead ends; product manager countered that it is a fallback and secondary to the app-to-app flow, so it does not move their verdict.
Whether the missing demo blocks approval: general user and product manager both called it a gap yet stayed useful; UX designer cited exactly that absence as the reason for staying unsure.

The unverified WebRTC off-LAN path: product manager flagged it as the one thing they could not confirm and still voted useful; the senior engineer raised related unanswered questions about server deployment and file sizes but treated them as non-blocking.
top_changes: Add a first-run walkthrough with screenshots or a short video of the app itself — launch, Send tab, files selected, device appears, progress, received — which is the single item the UX designer named as their blocker and which the general user and product manager also requested.

Rewrite the setup and troubleshooting guidance symptom-first with a plain-language, one-action recovery path, replacing 'disable AP isolation on your router' and raw firewall port instructions; this is the general user's stated asterisk and the product manager's second request.

Make README Getting Started internally consistent: one canonical command (fold the fvm note in or drop it), and either add `dart run build_runner build -d` as a numbered step or state when it is actually needed.
